edition_original: Harvard Semitic Series 5 (E. Chiera, Excavations at Nuzi I, 1929; 'Texts of Varied Contents'), whose documents Speiser transliterates and translates; the HSS 5 67 text itself was NOT read by A6 (archive.org OCR of HSS 5 contains only introduction and descriptions)

licence: archive.org metadata for item in.gov.ignca.4563 shows licenseurl: None and rights: None. The OCR text itself shows no licence. Speiser's name is confirmed on the BAS endnote and in Selman's footnote, not on the OCR title page.
notes: Quotes come from OCR text; OCR errors (e.g. 'fiistbom', 'Kosehaker') were corrected only where the sense is unambiguous. Page numbers are approximate because OCR running heads are garbled; the BAS endnote cites Speiser AASOR 10 pp. 7-13 for the adoption discussion. The article says Koschaker 'summed up' real adoption and that a son of the adoptive parent by his wife 'has the rights of the firstborn'. Selman (1974) cites HSS 5 67 as transliterated and translated in Speiser AASOR 10 No. 2 (WORK A6-W05 notes).

title_orig: The Social Environment of the Patriarchs (Tyndale Biblical Archaeology Lecture 1974)
title_es: El entorno social de los patriarcas
title_en: The Social Environment of the Patriarchs
author: M. J. Selman
genre: Scholarly lecture (Tyndale Bulletin) on Nuzi and Mesopotamian background to Genesis
licence: The PDF read shows no licence or copyright statement in the text extracted. Its licence status is UNVERIFIED by A6. Team must check the Tyndale Bulletin page before any publication.
notes: Running heads show pages 124-126 for the Eliezer discussion (p. 125 for the 'outsider could inherit' sentence, p. 126 for the Isaac/Eliezer difficulty). Selman's footnote 12 identifies HSS 5 67 as transliterated and translated in E. A. Speiser, AASOR 10 No. 2. Selman's footnote 14 lists HSS 5 67 among the 'maximum of six texts usually considered' as real adoption contracts. Selman's footnote 30 lists seven sistership-adoption-type contracts (including HSS 19 67) and says only two are actually entitled 'sistership adoption' (HSS 19 67 and JEN 78); this is a different text from HSS 5 67. Selman's footnote 46 says the practice of the adopted person's wife appears 'in HSS 5 67, though the wife's identity in this last text is not entirely clear'.

author: Lewis N. Dembitz; Kaufmann Kohler (as printed in the article header)
licence: The page read shows no licence statement; it carries 'About Jewish Encyclopedia' links. Public domain by date (1901-1906, team list); the page itself does not state it.
notes: Article contains: 'There is, however, one passage in Scripture (Gen. xlviii. 5)...'; 'Adoption in the Roman sense did not exist among the ancient Hebrews'; and 'the mode of Adoption being that the handmaid brought forth her child upon the knees of the adoptive mother (Gen. xxx. 3...)'. title_orig: Il papiro dell'adozione (Papiro Ashmolean 1945.96 - KRI VI 735-738)
author: Alberto Elli (article); original document Ramesside, reign of Ramesses XI (end of Dynasty 20)
date: Document: Ramesside (Ramesses XI, c. 1100 BCE); article: date not shown in the PDF read
language: Late Egyptian (document, as transliterated by Elli); Italian (Elli's article)
genre: Egyptian legal document: testamentary/adoption instrument of a childless couple
edition_original: Ashmolean Museum papyrus 1945.96; cited by Elli as KRI VI 735-738 (Kitchen, Ramesside Inscriptions). Not read by A6.
edition_english: Not read. A6 used Elli's Italian rendering (translated into English by A6; labelled as the team's translation).
licence: The PDF read shows no licence or copyright statement. Elli's article is in copyright (modern scholarship). A6 quoted only a short fragment of it in translation; team must confirm licence before publication.
notes: Elli cites A. H. Gardiner, 'Adoption extraordinary', JEA 26 (1940), pp. 23-29 for this papyrus; that article was NOT read. Elli says that normally, without a son, the wife's property passed to her brother and family, not to the husband's, and that the adoption kept it in the adoptive line. Elli also says the status of a slave's children depended on the father's acknowledgment of them.
